parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman asks about joining a sports centre.
script: Good afternoon, Parkside Sports Centre, Josh speaking.
Hello. I'm interested in joining the centre, and I'd like some information.
Of course. Can I take your name first?
Agnes Novak. N, O, V, A, K.
Thank you. We have two types of membership: full and off-peak. Full membership lets you come at any time. Off-peak is cheaper, but on weekdays you can only use the centre until four p.m.
I'm a student, so I can come during the day. Off-peak sounds right.
Off-peak membership is twenty-two pounds a month. Full membership is thirty-five.
Normally there's a fee of twenty pounds, but if you join before the end of May, there's no fee at all.
Great, I'll join this week then. What's included?
Every new member gets a free induction session with one of our trainers. They'll show you how to use the equipment safely and help you plan a programme.
Yes. Off-peak members can join yoga and dance classes at no extra cost. Boxing classes are only for full members, I'm afraid.
That's fine. Is there a swimming pool?
There is. It's open every day except Monday, when it's closed for cleaning.
What do I need to bring when I come to sign up?
Proof of address, such as a bank letter, and a photo for your membership card.
Yes, it's free for members for up to two hours.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A librarian speaks to new students about university library services.
script: Good morning, and welcome to the university library. My name's Ruth Okoro, and I'm one of the librarians here. I'll quickly explain how the library works.
First, the biggest change this year. Following requests from students, the library now stays open twenty-four hours a day during the exam periods. At other times, we close at midnight.
The ground floor is for group work, so you're allowed to talk there. The second and third floors are silent study areas, and phones must be switched to silent.
Food is not allowed anywhere in the library, but you may bring drinks in bottles with lids.
Most of our journals are now available online, so you can read them from home by logging in with your student account.
Now, borrowing. Undergraduates can borrow up to twelve books at a time, and the normal loan period is three weeks.
We don't charge fines any more. However, if you keep a book after its return date, your account will be suspended, and you won't be able to borrow anything else until it's returned.
If you'd like a group study room, you can book one for up to three hours using the library website.
Printing and photocopying are paid for using your student card, which you can top up at the machines by the entrance.
Finally, we run free workshops throughout the year on academic writing, including how to use references correctly. I strongly recommend them, especially in your first term.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: A student, Zara, discusses her dissertation with her tutor, Dr Hughes.
script: Come in, Zara. I've read the draft of your dissertation on ecotourism in Nepal.
Thank you. I'm worried it's not very good.
Actually, I think it's a solid start. The topic is well chosen. My main concern is that your research question isn't stated clearly enough at the beginning. A reader shouldn't have to search for it.
I see. I'll put it in the first paragraph.
Your interviews with guesthouse owners are the strongest part of the work. That's original data, and it's very valuable.
I was lucky. One of my cousins introduced me to most of them.
How many interviews did you do?
Fourteen. I planned twenty, but the trekking season ended earlier than expected.
Fourteen is fine. Now, what's your plan for the next month?
I was going to do more reading, but maybe I should focus on writing up the analysis first.
I agree. You've read plenty. The analysis is where your marks will come from.
Let's go through the chapters. Your introduction is fine, but it's too long. Cut it by about half.
The literature review is good, but it relies on sources that are mostly over twenty years old. You need some recent studies.
The content is fine, but the order is confusing. Describe how you chose the participants before you explain the interview questions.
That's excellent. Don't change anything there. But your short chapter on recommendations could be combined with the conclusion. It's only two pages.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on bamboo as a building material.
script: Today I'm going to talk about a material that has been used for thousands of years but is now attracting new interest from engineers: bamboo.
Although it looks like a tree, bamboo is actually a type of grass. And it grows astonishingly fast. Some species can grow nearly a metre in a single day.

This speed is one of its great advantages. A hardwood tree may take fifty years to reach a size suitable for building, but bamboo can be harvested after about four years, and it regrows from the same roots.

It's also extremely strong. In terms of tensile strength, that is, resistance to being pulled apart, some bamboo compares well with steel, which is why it's been used for scaffolding across Asia for centuries.
Environmentally, bamboo absorbs large amounts of carbon as it grows, and its extensive roots help prevent soil erosion on hillsides.

So why isn't it used more widely? Traditionally, the main problem has been durability. Untreated bamboo is easily attacked by insects and can rot within a few years. Today, however, it can be protected by soaking it in a solution containing boron, which is cheap and non-toxic to people.
Engineers have also developed engineered bamboo, made by pressing strips of bamboo together with glue to form beams and boards of standard sizes, which can be used like timber.
There are some impressive examples of modern bamboo architecture, such as a school in Bali whose classrooms are built almost entirely from bamboo.
The biggest remaining barrier is regulation. In most countries, there are no building codes for bamboo, so architects and insurers are reluctant to use it in large projects.

passages.title: A Brief History of the Umbrella
paragraphs: The umbrella is so familiar that it is easy to forget it was once a symbol of power. The earliest umbrellas, which appear in carvings from ancient Egypt and Assyria, were used to provide shade from the sun rather than shelter from the rain. They were carried by servants over the heads of kings and nobles, and ordinary people were not permitted to use them.

The Chinese are generally credited with being the first to make umbrellas waterproof. More than a thousand years ago, they began covering frames of bamboo with paper or silk treated with oil or wax. Umbrellas spread across Asia, where they also had religious and ceremonial uses, and elaborate designs indicated the rank of their owners.

In Europe, umbrellas were used in Italy and France by the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, but for a long time they were considered accessories for women. A man carrying an umbrella in the rain was thought weak or foolish. This began to change in London in the 1750s, thanks to a merchant and traveller named Jonas Hanway, who had seen umbrellas in Persia and began carrying one through the city's wet streets. He was frequently insulted by passers-by and especially by the drivers of hired carriages, who earned money from people trying to keep dry. Hanway ignored the insults for some thirty years, and by the time of his death in 1786, umbrellas had become common among London men.

Early European umbrellas were heavy and awkward, with frames of wood or whalebone. A major improvement came in 1852, when the English manufacturer Samuel Fox designed a frame with thin steel ribs. Fox had a large stock of steel originally intended for making corsets, and his new frame was both stronger and much lighter than earlier designs. Variations of his design are still used today.

The next important change made umbrellas easier to carry. In 1928 Hans Haupt, a German inventor, patented a telescopic pocket umbrella that could be folded into a much smaller size. Folding umbrellas became hugely popular in the second half of the twentieth century.

Today, more than a billion umbrellas are thought to be produced every year, many of them in the Chinese town of Shangyu, which is sometimes described as the umbrella capital of the world. Their low price, however, has an environmental cost. Most umbrellas are made from a mixture of metal, plastic and fabric that is difficult to separate for recycling, and because they are hard to repair, millions are thrown away after a single broken rib.

passages.title: Predicting Volcanic Eruptions
paragraphs: Around 800 million people live within 100 kilometres of an active volcano, many of them in densely populated countries such as Indonesia, the Philippines and Japan. For these communities, knowing when a volcano is likely to erupt can be a matter of life and death. Although scientists cannot yet predict eruptions with precision, monitoring has improved enormously in recent decades.

One of the most important tools is the seismometer, an instrument that detects vibrations in the ground. As magma rises beneath a volcano, it forces its way through rock, producing swarms of small earthquakes. A sudden increase in the number or strength of these earthquakes is often the first sign that a volcano is waking up. Networks of seismometers placed around a volcano allow scientists to track how deep the activity is and whether it is moving towards the surface.

Volcanoes also release gases, and changes in these gases can reveal what is happening underground. Scientists pay particular attention to sulphur dioxide and carbon dioxide, and to the ratio between them. Collecting samples near an active crater is extremely dangerous, so researchers increasingly use drones fitted with sensors, which can fly directly through volcanic plumes.

A third method involves measuring the shape of the volcano itself. When magma collects in a chamber beneath the surface, the ground above it can swell by a few centimetres. GPS instruments fixed on the volcano's slopes can detect these changes, and satellites using a radar technique known as InSAR can map tiny movements across entire regions, even in places that are too remote or dangerous for scientists to visit.

These methods have saved many lives. In 1991, scientists monitoring Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines recorded rising earthquake activity and gas emissions, and persuaded the authorities to evacuate tens of thousands of people. Days later, the volcano produced one of the largest eruptions of the twentieth century. Although hundreds of people died, scientists estimate that the evacuation prevented thousands of deaths.

Nevertheless, forecasting remains difficult. Every volcano behaves differently, and the signs of unrest do not always lead to an eruption. Some volcanoes show signs of activity for years without erupting, while others erupt with little warning. Repeated false alarms are costly and can make residents less willing to leave their homes the next time a warning is issued. For this reason, scientists now prefer to communicate risk in terms of probabilities and alert levels rather than precise predictions.

passages.title: The Multitasking Myth
paragraphs: Many of us are proud of our ability to multitask. We answer emails during meetings, check messages while studying and listen to podcasts while cooking. Job advertisements regularly ask for candidates who can handle several tasks at once. Yet decades of psychological research suggest that, for anything more demanding than walking and talking, true multitasking is largely an illusion.

When we believe we are doing two things simultaneously, the brain is usually switching rapidly between them. Each switch has a cost. In a well-known series of experiments published in 2001, the psychologists Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans showed that people took longer and made more errors when they alternated between tasks than when they completed one task before starting another. The delays from each switch may last only fractions of a second, but over a day they can add up to a substantial loss of productive time.

It might be expected that people who multitask frequently would become better at it. A 2009 study at Stanford University suggested the opposite. Researchers compared people who regularly used several forms of media at once with those who rarely did so. The heavy multitaskers performed worse on tests that required them to ignore irrelevant information and switch between tasks. Although the reasons are still debated, the finding challenges the idea that practice makes perfect in this area.

There are exceptions. In a 2010 study, David Strayer and Jason Watson asked participants to perform a driving simulation while solving memory and maths problems through a phone. Around 2.5 percent of participants showed no decline in performance. Strayer and Watson called them 'supertaskers'. Unfortunately, most people believe they belong to this small group, and in my view this overconfidence is a large part of the problem.

Even when we are not actively doing two things, distractions can harm performance. In one experiment, participants who simply received a phone notification during a task, without reading or answering it, made more mistakes than those who did not. The mere possibility of a message seems to pull part of our attention away from what we are doing.

What are the implications? Some companies offer training courses that claim to improve multitasking ability, but I see little convincing evidence that such training works. A better approach, I believe, is to design work so that people can concentrate. Employers should reduce unnecessary interruptions, for example by limiting meetings and allowing staff to switch off notifications for periods of focused work. For individuals, the advice is simple: whenever possible, do one thing at a time.

task1.text: The line graph below shows the number of visitors, in thousands, to three tourist attractions in one city between 2015 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The line graph shows how many people visited a castle, a science museum and a zoo in one city between 2015 and 2025.

Overall, all three attractions experienced a sharp fall in visitors in 2021, followed by a recovery. However, while the castle and the science museum ended the period with more visitors than at the start, the zoo's numbers remained well below their original level.

In 2015, the zoo was the most popular attraction, with 520,000 visitors, followed by the castle with 450,000 and the science museum with 300,000. Over the next four years, the castle and museum grew steadily, to 500,000 and 410,000 respectively, whereas the zoo declined slightly to 470,000.

In 2021, visitor numbers dropped dramatically at all three sites, to between 150,000 and 200,000. After this, the castle recovered strongly, reaching a peak of 560,000 in 2025, and the science museum rose to 450,000. In contrast, the zoo recovered only partially, reaching 350,000 in 2023 before falling slightly to 330,000, making it the least visited attraction.

task2.text: Many young people take a year off between finishing school and starting university, often to travel or work. Do the advantages of taking a gap year outweigh the disadvantages? Write at least 250 words.
model: In many countries, it has become common for school leavers to take a year off before university, often called a gap year. Although this decision carries some risks, I believe that, for most young people who plan it carefully, the advantages outweigh the disadvantages.

The main benefit of a gap year is personal development. After years of following school timetables, young people have the chance to take responsibility for their own lives, whether by working, volunteering or travelling. Someone who has worked in a café, organised a trip abroad or taught children in a rural school is likely to arrive at university more mature, more independent and more confident. A gap year can also help students choose the right course. Many first-year students drop out because they chose a subject without really knowing what interested them, and a year of experience can make that choice clearer.

There are, however, potential drawbacks. Some students lose the habit of studying and find it hard to return to academic work. Others may simply waste the year without a clear plan. Travelling can also be expensive, which means that gap years are more accessible to students from wealthier families, and those who stay at home may feel they are falling behind their friends.

These risks are real, but most of them can be reduced through planning. A gap year that combines paid work with some travel or volunteering, and includes a little reading related to the student's future course, can be affordable and keep the mind active.

In conclusion, although a gap year is not suitable for everyone, I believe a well-planned year away from formal education gives young people experience and maturity that make the disadvantages worth accepting.

speaking.cue:
Describe a park or garden that you like to visit.
You should say:
- where it is
- what it looks like
- what people do there
and explain why you like it.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to describe the Botanical Garden in Mirpur, in the northern part of Dhaka. It's quite a large place, and it's one of the few areas in the city where you can escape from the noise and traffic. When you walk in, the first thing you notice is how green it is. There are huge old trees, a small lake with water lilies, and several greenhouses with plants from different parts of the world, including cactuses and orchids. People use it in lots of different ways. In the early morning, you see older people walking or doing exercises. Later in the day, families come for picnics, and students like me go there to study under the trees or just chat with friends. I like it mainly because it calms me down. Dhaka can be very stressful, and after an hour in the garden I always feel more relaxed and able to think clearly. I'm also really interested in plants, so I enjoy reading the labels and learning the names of species I've never seen before. My only complaint is that it can get crowded on public holidays.
